articles.title: ‘Never underestimate the power of tucking’: how to make your spring wardrobe feel new without shopping
articles.summary: With a scarf, shirt, skirt or some clever cuffing, four fashion experts explain how you can achieve this season’s messy-but-chic look. Earlier this year I was having lunch with a friend who is a fashion buyer and trend forecaster.
body: Alongside the season’s other big looks – balloon pants, jaunty hats, the rogue use of scarves, knee-length skirts and underwear-as-outerwear – it’s clear the mood in fashion is messy-but-chic. Not quite the luxurious chaos of early 2000s boho, but similarly pretty and off kilter.

Thankfully, given the state of the economy and the environment, for the most part this style can be achieved by reaching into the dark corners of your wardrobe and looking at forgotten items with fresh eyes. Here, four fashion professionals explain how.

Figuring out exactly what is in your wardrobe is a worthwhile exercise at the change of seasons. Pull everything out and examine each item – this gives you the opportunity to rediscover pieces you’ve stopped wearing and to clean, mend or alter anything that could go back into rotation after a bit of love and care.
points: With a scarf, shirt, skirt or some clever cuffing, four fashion experts explain how you can achieve this season’s messy-but-chic look.

articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: in praise of slightly silly clothes
articles.summary: The push to buy lasting, sustainable clothes is a good thing, but every wardrobe need a bit of mischief. I do hope you are wearing your zebra stripe trousers today. Anyone who is anyone is wearing zebra stripes this month, you know.
body: Only teasing. Fashion doesn’t work like that any more. The days when people like me bullied everyone else into wearing banana yellow one season and puffball sleeves the next are over. Looking trendy is over. Timeless chic is the only show in town. Peacocking has been phased out in favour of understatement and personal style.

This is a very good thing. The fashion playbook that minted a whole new look every six months has a lot to answer for, seeding a sense of clothes as disposable that has got us into the right old mess that the industry is now in, with a glut of poorly made garments. Clothes that you never tire of, that you look after and repair because you want to wear them for ever, are obviously the holy grail of a sustainable wardrobe. When a look has the timestamp of a specific season – like Brat green in the summer of 2024 or Barbie pink the year before – it becomes a sell-by date. Clothes have a longer shelf life when their appeal isn’t based on novelty.
points: The push to buy lasting, sustainable clothes is a good thing, but every wardrobe need a bit of mischief.
I do hope you are wearing your zebra stripe trousers today.
Anyone who is anyone is wearing zebra stripes this month, you know.

articles.title: I tried to become a gay tradwife – and failed abysmally | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.summary: My sourdough starter died and my lone tomato nearly ruined me financially and emotionally. How did domestic drudgery and hard labour become an aspirational aesthetic? I have just eaten what may be the world’s most expensive tomato.
body: Of course, the tomato growing wasn’t really about saving money, it was about saving my sanity. Earlier this year, my wife and I got a plot at our local community garden; buoyed up by this development, I decided to ward off existential angst by throwing myself into tradwife-adjacent hobbies such as gardening and baking. I don’t know if it’s possible to be a gay tradwife but, after Googling the subject, I did find a magazine piece entitled The Curious Case of the Bisexual Tradwife. Alas, I can’t tell you much more about the phenomenon because there was a paywall. There are a lot of walls to pay in this life and this one did not make the cut.

While bisexual tradwives may be on the rise, my sourdough isn’t. I acquired some sourdough starter at a community garden fermentation and pickling workshop and, channelling my inner tradwife, I fed it religiously for a couple of weeks before I forgot about it and it died a pungent death. Nary a loaf was baked; the closest I got was buying some bread flour in the supermarket.
points: My sourdough starter died and my lone tomato nearly ruined me financially and emotionally.
How did domestic drudgery and hard labour become an aspirational aesthetic?

articles.title: Eric Idle has had tons of celebrities staying at his house. God, it must be exhausting | Adrian Chiles
articles.summary: Whether it’s an A-lister or an old schoolfriend emerging blearily from the spare room, those first moments of the day are tricky. First thing in the morning, that’s the hardest time. Eric Idle told me this. A wise man, is Eric.
body: This isn’t an issue raised in the book, which I should say is a moving, elegiac affair, and not just a torrent of name-drops as I’ve rather implied. But the guest question nagged away at me until I plucked up the courage to interrogate Mr Idle on the matter. Who was the best guest? Who was the worst? And what did he do if they were getting on his wick? After all, since they’d gone all that way, he could hardly turf them out.

Sensibly, Eric wouldn’t be drawn on any of these questions, although much as he plainly loved them being there, he did tacitly admit that having guests in your space – even guests of this calibre – does have its challenges, and that it’s the mornings that are hardest.

articles.title: How Himkok, One of the World’s Best Bars, Cultural Exchanges Are Key
articles.summary: This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. This is the second installment of our series Getting on the Map, presented by Apple Maps.
body: For the Oslo bar, sharing experiences—rather than just drinks—is the superior way to connect with other bartenders and gain some brand recognition along the way.

Guest shifts—where visiting bartenders pop up at host bars to serve signature drinks or collaborate on a limited-edition menu—are ubiquitous if you live in a city with a popular nightlife scene. But in recent years, some figures in the industry have been criticizing the practice. Complaints include the fact that they can be confusing to guests, dilute the quality of both teams’ drinks, and sometimes prioritize brands and influencers over loyal regulars.

After a few experiences with their own guest shifts, the team behind Oslo’s Himkok knew they wanted to do something different. Their solution, dubbed Nordic Sessions, aimed to address the criticism of the typical bar takeover, create more genuine connections between people in the industry, and spread the word about their bar and the products they use and love. I asked Himkok’s head of R&D Paul Aguilar how it works.

articles.title: An Afternoon of Skincare With Bluemercury and SkinCeuticals
articles.summary: At an event in Chestnut Hill, MA, customers gathered for skin analyses, personalized treatment plans, and a masterclass led by a SkinCeuticals pro.
body: There are many things you can do in Boston. You can wander through the historic Beacon Hill; you can catch a Red Sox game at Fenway Park; you could even go on a makeshift food tour in search of the perfect lobster roll. But for the skin-care obsessed, your interest might take you to the Chestnut Hill Bluemercury store for an exclusive masterclass with SkinCeuticals; or at least, that’s what happened to me—my ideal kind of Thursday afternoon.

As Bluemercury’s managing director of brand & communications Brooke Goodwin-Fullerton, tells me, moments like this one—combining of expertise, personalized service, and connection—is at the heart of the retailer. “Beauty is inherently sensorial, and that aspect of the experience can be lost while shopping online,” she says, whereas in store, you get a better idea how the formulas feel, and chat with its Beauty Experts along the way. “Our goal is for every client to leave feeling supported, more knowledgeable, and more confident about their beauty routine, but also that they’ve had a genuinely personalized experience.”

articles.summary: During pre-show cocktails in the Grand Tier Bar, Sigourney Weaver chatted with Frances McDormand as Katie Holmes arrived with her artist beau, Jason Bard Yarmosky. Gina Gershon, Julianna Margulies, Ellen Burstyn, Edmund Donovan, and Juliana Canfield—in vintage Tom Ford-era Yves Saint Laurent—were…
body: Something wicked this way hums. A wild and sumptuous new production of Verdi’s Macbeth brought out a bevy of stars and patrons on Tuesday evening, ready to celebrate the opening night of the Metropolitan Opera’s 141st season.

After a particularly melodious rendition of the national anthem—count on the Met audience to go full voice—the curtain soon rose on the Scottish Highlands. In this Louisa Proske-directed production, which opens with a jaw-dropping fight scene where sparks literally fly, the baritone Quinn Kelsey stars as the titular Scot, with powerhouse soprano Lise Davidsen by his side as the infamously scheming Lady Macbeth.

An early Verdi work based on the Shakespeare play, it is the story of the doomed Scottish nobleman, driven by a witch’s prophecy and his wife’s ruthless ambition to murder the king and take the throne. Over the course of five acts and Verdi’s moody score, Macbeth is ravaged by guilt and paranoia, though he continues to kill to preserve his ill-gotten crown before ultimately being vanquished by his countrymen’s rebel army.

articles.title: The Best Dressed Stars From Vogue World 2026: Milano
articles.summary: Tonight, A-list celebrities hit the Vogue World red carpet in their finest Milan-worthy looks. See who’s looks made our list of best dressed of the night.
body: Buongiorno, fashion lovers: Tonight, the Vogue World 2026: Milano show took over the Italian city’s famed Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II. And what a spectacle it was!

The stylish affair—which celebrated fashion’s ability to “preserve heritage, drive innovation, and shape the future”—featured a number of custom-made looks and runway cameos. And better yet, it also featured an expectedly starry front row.

Shortly before the thematic fashion displays came down the catwalk, A-list celebrities—such as Dakota Johnson, Jennifer Lopez, and Hunter Schafer—all hit the step and repeat in their Milan-worthy finest. Watching the Vogue World: Milano red carpet unfold was almost as much fun as the show itself.

Highlights included the black, full-skirted Dolce & Gabbana ballgown that Lopez donned on the red carpet (just moments before she hit the runway, no less). The hits by Italian labels then kept on coming: Stars like Hunter Schafer went sleek in a Prada two-piece, while Dakota Johnson opted for a black sheer Valentino number.

articles.title: All the Star Athletes Who Walked Vogue World 2026: Milano
articles.summary: From modern tennis legends like Aryna Sabalenka to Italian Olympians like Arianna Fontana, the Vogue World runway was replete with sports stars.
body: Last night, Vogue World 2026: Milano took place inside the historic Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, making for a joyous celebration of craft and style. A star-studded crowd witnessed the fifth installment of the global event, with the runways just as replete with names from across the worlds of art, music, film, fashion, and sport.

It made sense that sport should have its moment on the Vogue World runway. Fashion and athletics have long shared a vocabulary of performance and precision—and nowhere more visibly than in Italy, where houses from Prada to Armani have repeatedly blurred the line between sporting uniform and high style.

Italian volleyball player and Olympian Myriam Sylla wore a cobalt blue striped Miu Miu resort 2018 bodysuit, while her fellow champion Paola Egonu wore a similar set in a vibrant shade of Modena yellow.

Arianna Fontana—the Olympic short track speed skater, first woman to win Olympic medals in six straight Winter Olympics, and Italy’s most decorated athlete—shimmered in a bright orange, thick fringed dress with an olive sports jacket atop, the look completed with her own medals.
points: From modern tennis legends like Aryna Sabalenka to Italian Olympians like Arianna Fontana, the Vogue World runway was replete with sports stars.
